review_notes: I read the whole file and grepped Mathlib for uses of toCircle_intCast, toCircle_natCast, stdAddChar_apply, stdAddChar_coe and rootsOfUnityAddChar_val. I did not open the ZMod.natCast_val or natCast_zmod_val statements, so the interaction I describe with the `-ZMod.natCast_val` simp argument is inferred from how the proof uses them. I could not run Lean, so I make no claim about observed simp behaviour. Both findings are modest, and the lemma attributes are plausibly deliberate.

findings.excerpt: lemma stdAddChar_apply (j : ZMod N) : stdAddChar j = ↑(toCircle j) := rfl
findings.problem: `stdAddChar_apply` is the canonical unfolding of `stdAddChar` to `toCircle`. It is not tagged `@[simp]`, so every user has to name it explicitly. Three downstream proofs do this: `simp only [dft_apply, stdAddChar_apply, ...]` in Analysis/Fourier/ZMod.lean, `simp only [sum_mul, mul_sum, smul_eq_mul, stdAddChar_apply, ← mul_assoc]` in LSeries/ZMod.lean, and a `rw [..., stdAddChar_apply, ...]` in Fourier/ZMod.lean. The interface also has two other normal forms for the same term. `stdAddChar_coe` rewrites `stdAddChar (j : ZMod N)` to an explicit `exp`. The `AddChar.compAddMonoidHom_apply` route used by `toCircle_intCast` rewrites it the other way. Nothing says which form simp should produce.
findings.proposed_change: Decide on one normal form and record it. Either mark `stdAddChar_apply` `@[simp]` (the RHS is a bare coercion of a character value, so the rewrite terminates), or add a docstring saying it is deliberately left non-simp. If the attribute is added, the `simp only [..., stdAddChar_apply, ...]` call sites could use plain `simp`, though I have not checked that they would still close.
findings.benefit: Readers and users of `stdAddChar` get one canonical form (`↑(toCircle j)`) from simp, and downstream proofs no longer have to remember to pass this lemma by name.

evidence.excerpt: simp only [sum_mul, mul_sum, smul_eq_mul, stdAddChar_apply, ← mul_assoc]

findings.problem: The proof reverses `toCircle_natCast` (`← ZMod.toCircle_natCast`) and removes the simp lemma `ZMod.natCast_val` (`-ZMod.natCast_val`) by hand. It then re-adds `ZMod.natCast_zmod_val` to cancel the cast of `j.val`. That is a sign that the interface for `toCircle` applied to a casted `ZMod.val` is awkward. `toCircle_natCast` has the cast on the left and `exp (2 * π * I * j / N)` on the right, and the file uses it in both directions: backwards at line 143 and forwards at line 148, where `simp [..., ZMod.toCircle_natCast, mul_div_assoc]` needs `mul_div_assoc` to match the shape. The `exp (2 * π * I * ↑j.val / ↑N)` form produced by `toCircle_apply` is the same expression that `ZMod.natCast_val` would rewrite, so the two collide.
findings.proposed_change: State the evaluation lemma for the `exp` side in the form the downstream proofs consume, and give it a purpose-built simp lemma. One option is a lemma `(toCircle j : ℂ) = exp (2 * π * I * j.val / N)` (the coercion of `toCircle_apply`) with a `@[simp]` or `@[simp, norm_cast]` attribute, so that line 143 reduces to `simp`. Alternatively, restate `rootsOfUnityCircleEquiv_comp_rootsOfUnityAddChar_val` with the `ZMod.cast`-free `toCircle` value and drop the `-ZMod.natCast_val` argument.
findings.benefit: Removes the manual simp-set surgery and the back-and-forth use of `toCircle_natCast`. The proofs become robust if `ZMod.natCast_val` changes, and a new reader does not have to work out why that lemma is excluded.
